title: MITRE ATT&CK Investigation

theory.concept: ATT&CK is a catalogue of adversary behaviour organised as tactics (the goal: initial access, execution, persistence, privilege escalation, defence evasion, credential access, discovery, lateral movement, collection, command and control, exfiltration, impact) and techniques (the method, with an ID such as T1059.001). Mapping an incident to ATT&CK produces a shared vocabulary and exposes coverage gaps.
theory.why: A mapped incident can be compared against detection coverage, against other incidents and against the actor's known repertoire. Unmapped incidents produce reports nobody can act on.
look: One observed behaviour maps to exactly one technique - resist mapping the same event to five IDs
Sub-techniques where the evidence supports the specificity, parent technique where it does not
Tactics with no observed technique - either the attacker skipped the stage or you have a visibility gap
Techniques the actor is known for that you did NOT observe - a hunting hypothesis
fp: Mapping intent rather than evidence inflates the report; map what the logs show
A technique observed once by an automated tool is not the same as sustained operator tradecraft
tips: Build the mapping from your timeline, one event at a time, rather than from memory of the actor profile.
An empty tactic column is a finding worth writing down.

case.alert: ATT&CK mapping of the Northwind intrusion for the incident report
case.brief: Map each confirmed observation to the correct tactic and technique. The mapping goes into the incident report and drives the coverage assessment.

questions.label: Which ATT&CK tactic was NOT observed in this incident?
questions.hint: Read the coverage worksheet - one tactic is marked not observed.

questions.label: Given the actor profile, what does the absence of that tactic most likely mean?
questions.hint: TA-4411's profile places data theft before extortion, and you are on day two of a four-to-seven day dwell.

recommend.text: Publish the ATT&CK mapping with the incident report, overlay it against current detection coverage to expose gaps, and treat the absent Impact tactic as an expected next stage rather than good news.

hints: Map from evidence, not from intuition. Take each observation and ask which single technique the logged behaviour demonstrates.
The reference panel contains exactly the techniques you need, plus a few extras. Match by the behaviour described, not by keyword similarity.
review: Eleven of twelve tactics were observed - Initial Access through Exfiltration - which alone characterises this as a complete, human-operated intrusion rather than commodity malware. The mappings that matter most: T1562.001 for the AMSI bypass (defence evasion is often under-reported), T1574.011 for the service permissions escalation, T1003.006 for DCSync (the single most severe technique in the incident, because it puts every credential in the domain in the attacker's hands), T1090.001 for the internal pipe relay, and T1621 for the MFA push bombing. Impact is the only absent tactic, and that is not reassurance: TA-4411's profile places data theft before extortion, and you are on day two of a typical four-to-seven day dwell. The mapping's real value is the overlay against detection coverage, which is where the Linux telemetry gap and the missing .lnk-execution rule become visible as organisational findings rather than analyst opinions.
next: Technical analysis is complete. The incident manager now needs a response plan: what gets contained, in what order, and what has to be true before the business can be told it is over.

title: Incident Response

theory.concept: Incident response follows a lifecycle: preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, and lessons learned. Containment is usually staged - short-term actions to stop the bleeding, then longer-term isolation while evidence is preserved. Eradication removes attacker access; recovery restores service with monitoring in place to catch a return.
theory.why: Sequencing is everything. Eradicating before you have scoped leaves persistence behind; containing loudly before you have mapped every channel tells the operator to burn their infrastructure and dig in deeper.
look: Whether scoping is genuinely complete before eradication begins
Evidence preservation ahead of any action that destroys it - memory before power-off, disk images before rebuild
Credential invalidation that actually covers what was stolen, including Kerberos keys after DCSync
Whether containment actions are simultaneous where the attacker has multiple channels
Recovery criteria defined in advance, not negotiated under pressure
fp: Not every incident needs full crisis handling; over-response has real business cost
Rebuilding hosts that were only exposed, not compromised, wastes capacity
tips: Capture volatile memory before isolating or shutting down a host.
After DCSync, krbtgt must be reset twice with sufficient interval for replication - once is not enough.

case.alert: Response plan approval for the Northwind intrusion
case.brief: Sequence the response. The incident manager will execute exactly what you specify, in the order you specify it. Identify the correct ordering and the errors in the draft plan prepared by another analyst.

evidence.name: Confirmed Scope

Compromised accounts: svc_backup, deploy, m.chen (cloud+endpoint), svc_backup2 (attacker-created), plus all domain credentials via DCSync
Persistence: 6 mechanisms across 3 hosts (Run key, scheduled task, service, WMI pair, cron, SSH key) - HR01/SQL01 pending enumeration
C2 channels: HTTPS 600s, HTTPS 3600s long-sleep, DNS TXT tunnel, internal SMB named pipes
Data: ~344MB staged, confirmed exfiltration, 1,840 employees in scope
Not compromised: SRV-PCI01 (blocked by segmentation), WKS-2077 (exposed only), SOC-ANALYST-VM01 (SOC-owned)

Step 2: Reset m.chen's password
Step 3: Delete svc_backup2 from Active Directory
Step 4: Block 91.203.5.12 at the firewall
Step 5: Rebuild WKS-2041 from the standard image and return it to the user

IR-P-02 Containment across multiple channels must be executed simultaneously to prevent adversary adaptation
IR-P-03 Attacker-created accounts are disabled and preserved, never deleted, until forensics completes

questions.hint: Read IR-P-01 and consider what a power-off destroys permanently.

questions.hint: IR-P-04, plus recall what the attacker registered on that account.

questions.label: What is wrong with Step 3?
questions.hint: Read IR-P-03.

questions.hint: Count how many channels exist in the confirmed scope.

questions.label: What is wrong with Step 5?
questions.hint: Two hosts still have persistence enumeration pending, and rebuilding one host while the others beacon achieves nothing.

questions.label: How many times must krbtgt be reset, per policy?
questions.hint: Read IR-P-05.

questions.label: What is wrong with the closure criterion in Step 7?
questions.hint: IR-P-06 explicitly rejects this criterion - and recall the 3600-second long-sleep channel.

questions.label: Per policy, within how many working days must lessons learned occur?
questions.hint: Read IR-P-07 and compare with Step 8.

questions.label: Which single action should happen FIRST across the whole response?
options: Capture volatile memory from in-scope hosts
accept: capture volatile memory from in-scope hosts
questions.hint: Preservation precedes action for anything that destroys evidence.

recommend.text: Reject the draft plan: capture memory first, then execute simultaneous containment across all four channels and five hosts, disable rather than delete svc_backup2, revoke sessions and remove the attacker MFA device alongside resets, reset krbtgt twice, define recovery criteria in advance, and schedule lessons learned within 10 working days.

hints: Check the draft against the policy extract line by line. Almost every step violates one policy clause.
Two principles drive the correct order: preserve before you act, and act on every channel at once.
review: Every step of the draft is wrong in an instructive way. Powering off SRV-FILE02 destroys memory that holds the C2 configuration, injected code and possibly the archive password (IR-P-01). Resetting m.chen's password without revoking sessions and removing the attacker-registered MFA device leaves the intruder logged in (IR-P-04). Deleting svc_backup2 destroys evidence that should be disabled and preserved (IR-P-03). Blocking one IP leaves the long-sleep channel, the DNS tunnel and the internal pipe relay running (IR-P-02). Rebuilding one workstation before HR01 and SQL01 have even been enumerated is eradication before scoping. One krbtgt reset is insufficient after DCSync (IR-P-05). Absence of beaconing is explicitly not a closure criterion - a 3600-second implant designed to sleep through exactly this moment makes that obvious (IR-P-06). And 90 days for lessons learned is nine times the policy limit. Memory capture comes first.
next: Containment is executing. Forensics now needs artefacts from SRV-FILE02 to establish exactly what ran and when, including activity the logs never recorded.

title: Digital Forensics Investigation

theory.concept: Forensics recovers evidence from disk and memory artefacts, including things no log recorded. On Windows: prefetch (execution evidence), ShimCache and AmCache (programs present), $MFT and USN journal (file creation and deletion), SRUM (network usage per process), event log files themselves, registry hives, volume shadow copies, and memory for injected code and network state. Order of volatility governs collection: memory first, then disk.
theory.why: Attackers delete files and clear logs. Forensic artefacts survive both, and they are what makes findings defensible if the matter reaches lawyers or regulators.
look: Prefetch entries for binaries that no longer exist on disk, with run counts and last-run times
ShimCache/AmCache entries proving presence even without execution
USN journal records of file creation and deletion with timestamps
Timestamp anomalies - a $STANDARD_INFORMATION time earlier than $FILE_NAME indicates timestomping
Event log gaps: a cleared log leaves 1102, and an absence of records is itself evidence
fp: Prefetch proves execution, not malice - legitimate software appears there too
Antivirus quarantine and software uninstalls also delete files
tips: Maintain chain of custody with hashes of every image and artefact.
Compare $STANDARD_INFORMATION and $FILE_NAME timestamps whenever a file's dates look convenient.

case.alert: Forensic artefact review of SRV-FILE02 disk and memory image

recommend.text: Preserve all images and shadow copies under chain of custody, reset adm.tovar and every credential cached on the host, rebuild SRV-FILE02 rather than cleaning it, and record the anti-forensic activity in the incident report.

hints: Attackers delete files and clear logs; forensics is largely the study of what survives those actions anyway. Work through each artefact asking what it proves that the live system no longer does.
One binary in these artefacts was staged but never run, and one file has two different creation dates. Both are deliberate.
review: The artefacts survive every anti-forensic action taken. Prefetch proves nwsync.exe ran fourteen times between 09:44 on 4 March and 13:02 on 5 March even though the binary was deleted, and AmCache independently corroborates its presence. stage.exe appears in ShimCache with no prefetch entry: staged for a later phase, never executed - almost certainly the next-stage tool, and its absence from execution is why the Impact tactic was never observed. The $MFT shows svc.exe with $STANDARD_INFORMATION backdated to 2021 while $FILE_NAME records 2026-03-04 09:42:05, a timestomp intended to survive a sort-by-date review. The Security log was cleared at 13:05:40 on 5 March by svc_backup2, but the 00:30 shadow copy preserved both the records and all three deleted archives. Memory delivers what no log held: an injected RWX region in explorer.exe, live C2 and internal pipe connections, the archive password in plain text, the operator's command history including 'reg save HKLM\SAM', and cached credentials for adm.tovar - exposed simply because that administrator logged on to a compromised host during an unrelated support ticket.
next: Every host is understood individually. Assemble them into a single correlated narrative across the whole estate, with a timeline that an executive and a regulator can both follow.

title: Multi-Stage Attack Investigation

theory.concept: A multi-stage investigation correlates evidence from several hosts, identities and data sources into one narrative: how the attacker entered, how each stage enabled the next, and where the defence succeeded or failed. The output is a single timeline that survives cross-examination.
theory.why: Individually investigated hosts produce a list of incidents. Correlated, they produce the actual story - and the story is what drives remediation funding and regulatory position.
look: Causal links: each stage must be explained by the one before it
Two intrusion paths converging on one identity or host
Time gaps that indicate operator working hours or handoffs between teams
Controls that worked - they belong in the report as prominently as the failures
The earliest point at which existing telemetry could have caught it
fp: Coincidental timing is not causation - require an artefact linking the stages
An event during the incident window is not automatically part of the incident
tips: Build the timeline in UTC and state the timezone explicitly.
For every stage, name the control that should have stopped it and why it did not.

hints: Two intrusion paths ran in parallel for most of 4 March. Find the single event where an artefact from one path is used on a host from the other.
The most important finding is not technical. An alert was correctly escalated on 2 March and nothing was blocked for 44 hours.
review: One actor, two parallel paths, converging by design. Path A was a noisy perimeter credential attack that produced a Domain Admin backdoor. Path B was a quiet, targeted phishing campaign using infrastructure registered on 24 February - eight days before the first probe, which shows planning. The paths converged at 10:18 on 4 March when svc_backup2, created via Path A on the domain controller, exercised privileges on SRV-FILE02, a Path B host: from that point the attacker held both a domain-level identity and SYSTEM on a data-rich server, which is what made DCSync and estate-wide movement possible. Shared infrastructure (one /24, one registrar, one set of nameservers), shared tooling artefacts (mutex, user-agent, JA3) and the convergence itself put attribution to one actor beyond reasonable doubt. Four controls worked and belong in the report: PCI segmentation, volume shadow copies, one user reporting the phish, and script block logging. But the defining finding is organisational rather than technical - NW-8841 was correctly escalated on 2 March at 06:12 and no perimeter block was applied for 44 hours, during which the same address walked in through an ownerless 2021 firewall rule.
next: The incident is contained and understood. Before you are cleared for the master assessment, demonstrate that you can run the operational side of a SOC: hunting, metrics, tuning and shift discipline.

title: Advanced SOC Operations

theory.concept: Mature SOCs do more than work a queue. Threat hunting tests hypotheses against data where no alert exists. Metrics (time to detect, time to triage, time to contain, false positive rate, detection coverage) show whether the function is improving. Purple teaming validates detections against real technique execution. Shift handover, case documentation and escalation discipline keep it all coherent across people and time.
theory.why: Detection engineering fixes what you have already seen. Hunting and validation address what you have not, and metrics tell you honestly whether either is working.
look: Hypotheses that are specific, data-backed and falsifiable - not 'look for anything weird'
Metrics that measure outcomes rather than activity; alerts closed per analyst is not a quality measure
Coverage measured against a framework rather than against the vendor's rule count
Handover notes that a stranger could act on
fp: Hunts without a hypothesis generate findings nobody can interpret
A low false positive rate can simply mean the rules are too narrow to fire
tips: Every hunt ends in one of three outcomes: a finding, a new detection, or a documented negative result. All three are valuable.
Measure time to contain, not just time to detect - the gap between them is where damage happens.

recommend.text: Institute mandatory ownership and an action SLA for every escalation, run H1, H2, H4 and H5, commission purple team validation of the three untested techniques, drive the FP rate down through the tuning backlog, and close the Linux telemetry gap.

hints: Read the metrics as a story about where time went. Detection was instant; something between detection and action consumed two days.
A usable hunt hypothesis names the data source it will be tested against and can come back negative. Two of these cannot.
review: Detection performed well - the alert fired in the same minute as the first malicious activity, and triage and escalation were correct within 63 minutes. Everything after that is the problem. No owner was assigned to the resulting perimeter action, so the same address walked in 44 hours later through a rule nobody owned either; F1 is the highest-impact finding in the entire incident and it is a process failure, not a technology one. It is compounded by F5: the handover notes never mentioned NW-8841, so the next shift had no reason to chase it. A 62 percent false positive rate means analysts spend most of their shift on noise, which is precisely the condition under which a two-day-old escalation gets forgotten. Coverage of 9 of 21 observed techniques, an 18-month gap in purple team validation of the three techniques most central to this intrusion, and 40 percent Linux telemetry complete the picture. H1 and H5 hunt this actor; H2 and H4 hunt the class of weakness that let them in, which is the more durable investment. H3 is untestable and H6 is unfalsifiable.
